The customer volunteers a raw, extensive financial hardship disclosure — back taxes, threatened home sale, borrowed money — that the setter acknowledges only with a brief 'I'm sorry about that' before the call ends in a DQ. Energy leaked steadily from the neighbor-interest opening to a resigned goodbye.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: empathy during vulnerability disclosure on a DQ call
primary_coaching_focus.quote: a lot of stuff just happened. I've lived here seventeen years, and out of nowhere, they've told me that I owe them with $15,000 in taxes.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The customer hands over an unusually raw, extended financial hardship disclosure and the setter offers almost no verbal acknowledgment until the call is already ending. Per coaching_philosophy.empathy_on_vulnerability_disclosure this is a trust-gift moment independent of whether the deal closes, and the rep's near-silence through it is the most consequential, coachable gap on this call.

key_moments.stewart_read: A $300/month bill is a strong pain anchor and the setter reacted well in the moment, but the call never got the chance to use it since the credit DQ arrived one exchange later.

key_moments.quote: Okay. I know how much it is. And if that's a part of it, my credit is not good, and I won't be able to, like, get a loan for this at all.
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer is mid-disclosure of a severe financial hardship (a $15,000 surprise tax bill, threatened forced sale of his home of 17 years) and is essentially narrating his own disqualification in real time. The setter does not interject with any acknowledgment during this stretch.

key_moments.quote: Yeah. I'm sorry about that. Yeah. I tried to investigate it a little bit, but it couldn't get real far. So whatever.
key_moments.stewart_read: The only empathy offered across the entire ~90-second hardship disclosure is a four-word 'I'm sorry about that,' delivered right as the setter is also confirming the DQ. It reads as procedural closure, not genuine acknowledgment.

key_moments.quote: There's, so without a credit score over 670, there's nothing I can do?
key_moments.stewart_read: The setter confirms the hard credit DQ per script, correctly following the 670 threshold rule. This is procedurally correct — no alternative financing path is offered because the schema currently treats this as a hard_dq with no confirmed fallback.
